extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners addressing obviousness rejections)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103, implementing the Graham framework and KSR precedent for USPTO examination and Office actions. Covers factual inquiries, search scope, rationales for rejections, applicant replies, and consideration of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective analysis for determining obviousness is based on the Graham v. John Deere Co. factual inquiries: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Objective (secondary) evidence such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results must also be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these factors case-by-case; secondary considerations may be included in specification, on filing, or timely during prosecution; weight given is case-specific and not dispositive by mere submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders; requirement to articulate findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel fulfill the role of factfinder for the Graham inquiries, and must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of applied references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once factual findings are articulated, provide an explanation supporting an obviousness rejection in the Office action (35 U.S.C. 132 requires notification of reasons). Clear factual findings and rationale facilitate applicant response and prompt resolution; failure to follow guidelines is neither appealable nor petitionable, but rejections must be based on substantive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification and claims; determine claim scope by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.' Then determine what to search for and where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §904 for detailed search procedures. The search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search (analogous and nonanalogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search following general MPEP search guidelines. Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem; art from other fields can be considered when reasonably pertinent (analogous art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognizes that works from other fields or addressing different problems may prompt predictable variations; consult MPEP §2141.01(a) for analogous art discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole to ascertain differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §2111 claim interpretation principles and consider entire disclosures (MPEP §2141.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill. Factors include type of problems encountered, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovation, sophistication of technology, and educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every factor will be present; one or more may predominate. Examiners may rely on their technical expertise; a person of ordinary skill is also a person of ordinary creativity (KSR). If prior art itself reflects appropriate level, specifying a particular level may not be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing and articulating rationales to support obviousness rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: After resolving Graham factual inquiries, determine whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill and articulate the rationale(s) supporting that conclusion; offer reasoned explanation avoiding conclusory generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR requires explicit analysis. Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (cf. In re Kahn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A: Combining prior art elements for predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results may support an obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the combination does no more than yield predictable results from known elements and methods (KSR examples such as Anderson’s-Black Rock and Sakraida).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B: Simple substitution of known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results may support an obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the substituted element merely yields predictable results and does not supply a nonobvious improvement (cf. United States v. Adams guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products in the same way may support an obviousness conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would recognize the technique would improve similar devices in the same way, using the technique is obvious unless its actual application is beyond ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) that is ready for improvement to yield predictable results may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the device was 'ready for improvement' and whether the results would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E: 'Obvious to try' when finite predictable solutions exist
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' may support obviousness where choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions would have been made with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale requires identifiable, finite, and predictable options and a reasonable expectation of success; cannot be invoked where results are unpredictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F: Variations prompted by known work across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in the same or different field based on design incentives or market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR endorses considering cross-field analogies and market/design incentives where predictable variation would have been implemented by a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) as one valid rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine prior art teachings can support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM is a valid rationale and preferred to be identified when present; KSR cautioned against overly rigid TSM but did not eliminate it. If TSM exists, make it explicit; when lacking, other rationales can be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to consider all claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: All claim limitations must be considered in the obviousness analysis; the prior art reference(s) need not teach every limitation, but the examiner must explain why differences would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each limitation is addressed in the factual findings and rationale; the mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness (Dann v. Johnston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and necessity for evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense can be invoked to supply limitations or motivations, but must be supported by evidence and a reasoned explanation; more searching explanation required when the missing limitation goes to the heart of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on conclusory appeals to common sense; provide factual underpinnings or explanation showing why a person of ordinary skill would have used common sense in that way (Arendi v. Apple; DyStar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply obligations under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection; replies must present arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement that the Office has not made a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported is insufficient. If applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining the alleged error; otherwise the examiner may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants, including secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After rebuttal evidence is submitted, reconsider initial obviousness determinations in view of the entire record; review all rejections of record and proposed rejections and confirm continued viability. Follow MPEP §2145 and §§716–716.10 re: affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of applicant rebuttal arguments — inability to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may submit evidence demonstrating that one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If credible, examiners should reassess the prior obviousness finding and evaluate whether the asserted difficulties negate the asserted rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of applicant rebuttal arguments — combination performs more than separate functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may argue that the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately (i.e., the combination yields more than predictable aggregation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence for unexpected properties or synergistic effects; if present, consider weight as secondary consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of applicant rebuttal arguments — unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may present evidence that the claimed combination produced unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results are a form of secondary consideration that must be weighed in the obviousness analysis; reexamine rejections in view of such evidence (In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art availability under 35 U.S.C. 102 applies in 103 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§901–901.06(d), §§2121–2129 for what constitutes prior art; admitted prior art may be used even if it would not otherwise qualify under statutory categories.
